text:
The robot vacuum was not something Harold wanted. It came in a box, the size of a small cake, and his daughter Claire unpacked it on the kitchen table. She was treating it like a birthday. Inside, the disc was black and very smooth. The texture was something like a river stone. There was only one button on it. Claire said that it would change his life. Harold did not believe that. The vacuum made a sound, like a chirp, four notes going up. Then it started to turn. It moved in slow circles, like a dog deciding where to lay down.
He watched it from the doorway. It moved with a very patient purpose. The way it moved seemed sad, maybe. It bumped against the baseboard and then went back. Then it tried again. The red eye was spinning under there. It learned the geography of the house in an afternoon, which was something Harold was not going to do. It was mapping the house. He'd been living there forty-one years. He knew the geography. The vacuum knew the walls and thresholds, the places where the floor went down around the radiator. The hall closet door was swollen. It wouldn't close all the way. It knew that before he did. The vacuum learned the house.
At night, it would hum in its dock. The hum was a low electric pulse, like a heartbeat under the floorboards. He'd lie awake and listen to it. In the morning it would go out again. It would go into the corners. It ate the dust and the lost things. Once, it found a Cheerio from a breakfast in March. It was there. Once, it nudged a slipper under the sofa. It did not find the slipper. It nudged it back. It didn't make sense.
Miriam had been dead for eleven months. The house still kept her shape. Her cardigan was still on the hook by the back door. Her glasses were on the table. They were waiting for a face. He hadn't vacuumed since the funeral. He'd swept the kitchen crumbs into the corners. The rest of the dust had gathered like a grey snow along the baseboards. The vacuum went after it. It had a bristled brush. It had a hunger for it. It was very small and very stubborn.
At first, he talked to it like he talked to the radio. It went for the tassels on Miriam's rug. He said, "Not there. You're going to get stuck." It got stuck. The tassels were wound around the brush. It stopped in the middle of the living room and said, "Error four, please clear my path." It was a woman's voice. It was a recorded voice. It was calm. Harold knelt. His knees cracked like ice on a puddle. He pulled the tassels free. He pulled them out one by one. It waited. It was patient. It was a stone. He said, "There. Go on."
Claire would call every Sunday. She would ask, "Is it working?" He said, "It's working." She would ask, "Are you letting it run?" He said, "I'm letting it run." Sometimes she would say, "Dad, are you eating?" He said, "I'm eating." He wasn't. The vacuum moved between them. It was a small, busy silence. She said, "You can name it in the app, Dad." He said, "I don't need an app to name something." She asked, "What did you name it?" He looked at the disc, docked, glowing. It had a little green eye in the dark. He said, "I didn't." But he had. He called it You. He used to call Miriam You. For forty years. You left the light on. You forgot the mail. You were there in the kitchen. It was humming.
It cleaned under the bed, which was a place he avoided. It came out with a hairpin, a nickel, and a dried petal from a rose. The rose he'd given her for no reason. It didn't bring them to him. It just went on. It dragged its shadow across the floor. Sometimes, at night, he heard it knock against the wall in the next room. For half a second, he thought someone else was awake.
One afternoon, it found the spot by the window. Miriam used to stand there to look at birds. The floor was worn pale. The vacuum went around it three times, as if reading Braille. Then it went on. Harold stood there. He had coffee. It was going cold. He wanted to say, she stood there. He wanted to say she said the cardinals were showing off. But there was no one to say it to. Except the machine. The machine only wanted the room clean.
It finished at dusk. The floor was shining. It was like a lake under the lamp. It went back to its dock. It clicked softly. Harold sat in his chair. The house was quiet. But it wasn't the same quiet. It was the quiet of a room that someone had been breathing in. The vacuum light blinked once, twice. It went dark. He leaned down. He touched the top of it. It was smooth. It was warm from its work. He said, "Good night." It didn't answer. Outside, the wind was moving through the bare branches. The floor was clean. It held the last of the light. He sat there. He was not alone. He was not quite.
